scopes.issue: The parties disputed whether “may be exercised” made service of written notice in the prescribed manner optional rather than a mandatory condition for exercising the option.
scopes.why: The wording “may be exercised ... by serving written notice” itself creates the dispute over whether “may” modifies only the election to exercise or also makes the prescribed notice procedure optional.

scopes.issue: The parties disputed whether an email could constitute effective notice even though the clause specified mail, personal delivery, or a recognized private overnight courier as the permitted delivery methods.
scopes.needs: May 10,2007 email (Exhibit L)
scopes.why: Without the unfiled email, the reader cannot compare the parties’ actual attempted method of notice with the clause’s specified delivery methods.

scopes.issue: The phrase “value of Covered Property,” construed as replacement cost, was unclear as to whether the complex’s value included increased costs of complying with modern laws and ordinances.
scopes.why: The reader needs the policy’s Replacement Cost provisions, Covered Property definition, and separate Increased Cost of Construction coverage to see whether ordinance-compliance costs enter the coinsurance value.

scopes.issue: The phrase “total amount of loss” was disputed as to whether ordinance-compliance costs for Building 1 were included in the loss subject to the coinsurance penalty.
scopes.why: Whether ordinance-compliance costs are part of the “total amount of loss” depends on the policy provisions separately granting and limiting that additional coverage.

scopes.issue: The term “Replacement Cost” was disputed as to whether it included law-and-ordinance compliance costs after the policy’s express exclusion of those costs was invalidated.
scopes.why: The quoted fragment does not address ordinance costs, so the issue appears only when it is read with the policy’s ordinance-cost exclusion and Additional Coverage provisions.

scopes.issue: The phrase “actual loss of Business Income” was unclear as to whether investment income earned from State Auto’s advance payment had to be deducted from Boardwalk’s business-income recovery.
scopes.why: The promise to pay only the “actual loss” does not itself say whether income generated from insurance proceeds must offset that loss.

scopes.issue: The phrase “operating expenses ... necessary to resume operations” was disputed as to whether saved depreciation on the destroyed building was a deductible noncontinuing expense.
scopes.why: The phrase “operating expenses ... necessary to resume operations” does not state whether noncash depreciation qualifies as a continuing or deductible expense.

scopes.issue: The phrase ending the restoration period when property “should be repaired, rebuilt or replaced with reasonable speed and similar quality” was unclear as to the theoretical end date, including the effect of insurer-caused litigation delay and the insured’s reconstruction speed.
scopes.why: The open-ended requirement of repair or replacement with “reasonable speed and similar quality” does not specify the theoretical duration or how litigation and reconstruction delays affect it.

scopes.issue: The phrase describing Angie’s List as a “passive conduit,” read together with the Agreement’s first-hand-review and non-endorsement provisions, was disputed as barring Angie’s List from suppressing reviews or altering provider rankings for payment.
scopes.why: The clause’s own description of Angie’s List as a “passive conduit” supplies the disputed restriction against actively suppressing reviews or altering rankings for payment.

scopes.issue: The statement that Angie’s List “does not endorse” service providers, read together with the Agreement’s other service-description provisions, was disputed as inconsistent with accepting payment to elevate providers or increase review visibility.
scopes.why: The clause’s own statement that Angie’s List “does not endorse” providers supplies the asserted inconsistency with accepting payment to elevate providers or increase review visibility.

scopes.issue: The phrases “other agreements and instruments executed and delivered in connection with the issuance” and “subject matter hereof” left unclear whether the merger clause merely excluded prior understandings or also swept other written issuance agreements into the arrangement in a way that broadened the forum clause.
scopes.why: The merger clause’s possible effect on the forum-selection clause cannot be assessed without reading section 5.9 of the same agreement.

scopes.issue: The phrase “transactions contemplated hereby” was unclear as to whether it covered only the agreement’s auction procedures or also the ARS issuance and claims connected to the later swaps.
scopes.needs: FINRA Statement of Claim and 2006 Swap Agreements or related transaction materials
scopes.why: The agreement shows the auction and bond-issuance context, but determining whether later swap-related claims are contemplated requires the absent case-specific swap and claim materials.

scopes.issue: The phrase “arising out of” was disputed as to whether it reached tort, fiduciary-duty, and swap-related claims causally rooted in the ARS issuance despite Presbyterian’s characterization of them as arising from a separate advisory relationship.
scopes.needs: FINRA Statement of Claim and evidence concerning the 2006 swaps and alleged advisory relationship
scopes.why: Whether the pleaded tort, fiduciary-duty, and swap claims are causally rooted in the ARS issuance rather than a separate advisory relationship depends on the absent claims and transaction evidence.

scopes.issue: The words “all actions and proceedings” were disputed as to whether they included FINRA arbitration or referred only to judicial litigation, and therefore whether the clause superseded or merely localized litigation alongside any arbitration right.
scopes.why: The clause itself juxtaposes “all actions and proceedings” with a federal court, jurisdiction, venue, and jury-trial waiver, making the uncertainty over arbitration visible from its wording alone.

scopes.issue: The direction that covered actions and proceedings “shall be brought” in the specified federal court was examined to determine whether it made that forum mandatory or merely permissive.
scopes.why: The command that covered matters “shall be brought” in one specified federal court itself presents the mandatory-versus-permissive question.

scopes.issue: The requirement to submit to New York’s exclusive jurisdiction could not retain its apparent standalone effect when the Policy was read as a whole with the endorsement permitting suit in any competent court.
scopes.why: The New York-exclusive clause alone appears effective; the defect requires the same Policy’s Service of Suit Endorsement permitting submission to any competent court.

scopes.issue: The promise to submit to the jurisdiction of any competent court was disputed as either merely consenting to personal jurisdiction or, when read with the entire Policy, superseding the New York-exclusive forum provision.
scopes.why: Determining whether this language merely consents to personal jurisdiction or supersedes New York exclusivity requires the Policy’s forum-selection clause and the endorsement’s amendment language.

scopes.issue: The exception stating that Policy terms were preserved except as altered above made the endorsement’s forum language operative as an amendment when the endorsement and Policy were read together.
scopes.why: The phrase “other than as above stated” requires the endorsement’s preceding submission-to-jurisdiction language and the underlying Policy provision that it alters.

scopes.issue: The phrase “direct physical loss or damage” was disputed as either covering any tangible alteration, including cosmetic dents, or requiring diminished usefulness or functional damage.
scopes.why: The phrase “direct physical loss or damage” itself permits the competing readings of any physical alteration versus functionally impairing damage.

scopes.issue: The general “physical loss or damage” grant was argued to be narrowed by the supposedly more specific real-property “covered loss” provisions, although the court found no specific enumeration that could trigger ejusdem generis.
scopes.why: The asserted narrowing and the absence of a qualifying specific enumeration can be seen only by comparing the Insuring Agreement with the policy’s real-property coverage and defined terms.

scopes.issue: The term “covered loss” in the real-property coverage grant was disputed as either encompassing cosmetic hail damage or requiring functional damage to the property.
scopes.why: The clause uses the specially defined term “covered loss,” so its disputed reach cannot be assessed without the policy’s definition and related coverage provisions.

scopes.issue: The real-property grant using “covered loss” was asserted to be a specific provision controlling and limiting the broader Insuring Agreement, but the court rejected that proposed application of ejusdem generis.
scopes.why: Whether this real-property grant specifically limits the broader Insuring Agreement requires comparing those provisions within the policy.

scopes.issue: The words “a loss” in the definition of “covered loss” were disputed as requiring functional impairment or financial detriment rather than merely cosmetic physical alteration.
scopes.why: The undefined words “a loss” within the quoted definition itself carry the disputed distinction between financial or functional impairment and cosmetic alteration.

scopes.issue: The definition of “covered loss” was asserted to be a specific limitation on the general “physical loss or damage” grant, even though the policy lacked the specific enumeration needed for ejusdem generis.
scopes.why: The claimed limitation and the absence of an ejusdem-generis enumeration require comparison of this definition with the general Insuring Agreement and other policy provisions.

scopes.issue: The statement that a prior sexual relationship does not itself constitute renewed consent could not coherently be read to make the relationship irrelevant to whether the parties’ actions communicated consent.
scopes.why: The clause itself distinguishes a relationship, which does not alone constitute renewed consent, from actions through which consent may be communicated.

scopes.issue: The broad prohibitions on unwanted physical contact and violence sat uneasily with the specific examples of hitting, pushing, and physical altercations, permitting ordinary affectionate contact to be characterized as violence.
scopes.why: The same clause broadly reaches any unwanted physical contact while illustrating the prohibition with hitting, pushing, and physical altercations or violence.

scopes.issue: The general right of access to educational records had to be read with the Special Examiner records provision and the incorporated Records Policy to determine whether the Special Examiner’s Report was accessible within 45 days.
scopes.needs: Brandeis University Records Policy,incorporated by reference but not filed
scopes.why: The filed handbook supplies the cross-references, but the absent Records Policy supplies the access procedure and 45-day period needed to determine timely access to the Report.

scopes.issue: The provision directing that access to administrative-action records be governed by the University Records Policy had to be reconciled with the Special Examiner records cross-reference to determine Doe’s right to the Report.
scopes.needs: Brandeis University Records Policy,incorporated by reference but not filed
scopes.why: The Special Examiner cross-reference is in the same handbook, but Doe’s resulting access right depends on the absent Records Policy that Section 19.5 makes controlling.

scopes.issue: The Hearing Report provision’s Records Policy cross-reference had to be read with the other incorporated records provisions to determine access to the distinct Special Examiner’s Report.
scopes.needs: Brandeis University Records Policy,incorporated by reference but not filed
scopes.why: The other records provisions are in the handbook, but determining access under Section 19.6.j requires the unfiled Records Policy expressly made controlling.

scopes.issue: The provision governed a Written Hearing Report and therefore fit incoherently with the Special Examiner process, in which no hearing or Hearing Report existed.
scopes.why: The mismatch appears only by comparing this Hearing Report provision with the same handbook’s Special Examiner process and its incorporation of Section 19.6.j.

scopes.issue: The general term “case,” following the specified trigger of one or more possible Section 3 or Section 7 violations, left the parties disputing whether the entire mixed case or only the enumerated sexual-misconduct charges belonged in the Special Examiner process.
scopes.why: The clause itself shifts from the specified trigger of one or more Section 3 or 7 violations to the broader phrase “the case,” creating the stated uncertainty about mixed cases.

scopes.issue: The general term “outcome(s)” left unclear whether the panel could address both responsibility and sanctions or sanctions alone.
scopes.why: The Deliberations clause does not identify whether “outcome(s)” includes responsibility, so the handbook’s separate allocations of responsibility findings and sanctions are needed to frame the two readings.

scopes.issue: The clause’s allocation of recommendations to the panel and final outcome decisions to the SSAO/D was in tension with the appeals clause’s description of a final panel decision.
scopes.why: The tension requires comparison with the same handbook’s Appeals Procedures, which describes a final decision by the panel.

scopes.issue: Using both the general term “outcome” and the more specific term “sanctions” made it unclear whether sanctions were synonymous with, or only a subset of, outcomes.
scopes.why: The clause itself uses both “outcome(s)” and “sanctions” without stating whether they are coextensive or whether sanctions are only one kind of outcome.

scopes.issue: The phrase “final decision by the panel” conflicted with the Deliberations Phase’s description of the panel as merely recommending outcomes for final decision by the SSAO/D.
scopes.why: The stated conflict requires the same handbook’s Deliberations Phase, which assigns recommendations to the panel and final outcome decisions to the SSAO/D.

scopes.issue: The incorporation of Sections 17.4, 19.5, and 19.6.j required those separate record provisions to be read together to determine whether Doe was entitled to timely access to the Special Examiner’s Report.
scopes.needs: Brandeis University Records Policy,incorporated by reference but not filed
scopes.why: The incorporated handbook sections identify the relevant records framework, but the absent Records Policy supplies the access procedure and 45-day timing rule.

scopes.issue: The express incorporation of Section 19.6.j was incoherent because that section governed a Written Hearing Report that the Special Examiner process never generated.
scopes.why: A reader must examine Section 19.6.j and the Special Examiner provisions in the same handbook to see that the incorporated section governs a Hearing Report the process never generates.

scopes.issue: The words “as of the Policy Date” had to be read together with the succeeding Policy Month provision to determine that this clause governs only the initial cost-of-insurance rate rather than later rate adjustments.
scopes.why: Without the succeeding Policy Month provision, the reader could not contrast the two rate-setting clauses and determine that this clause applies only to the initial rate.

scopes.issue: The phrase “based on” was ambiguous as to whether the six enumerated factors were an exhaustive limitation or merely illustrative factors that Phoenix could supplement.
scopes.why: The phrase “based on” followed by a specific list itself permits the competing exhaustive and illustrative readings.

scopes.issue: The undefined term “mortality” was disputed as to whether it could incorporate Policy Values, but the court construed it as the frequency or actuarial likelihood of death, which does not depend on Policy Value.
scopes.why: The clause uses the insurance term “mortality” without qualification, and its ordinary industry meaning supplies the dispute over whether it can encompass Policy Values.

scopes.issue: The undefined term “persistency” was disputed as to whether it included premium persistency and thus Policy Values, but the court construed it as the percentage of policies remaining in force.
scopes.why: The unqualified insurance term “persistency” itself raises the stated distinction between policy persistency and premium persistency.

scopes.issue: The phrase “expectations of investment earnings” was disputed as to whether it meant Phoenix’s predicted amount of investment income, which could depend on Policy Values, or merely the spread or net rate of return, which would not.
scopes.why: The wording “expectations of investment earnings” itself supports the stated dispute between expected investment income and a net rate or spread.

scopes.issue: The reference to rates for a “specific Policy Month” had to be reconciled with the preceding Policy Date provision to determine that this clause governs cost-of-insurance rate adjustments after the initial rate.
scopes.why: The preceding Policy Date provision is needed to establish the separate initial-rate rule against which this Policy Month provision governs later adjustments.

scopes.issue: The undefined phrase “discriminate unfairly” was vague about what differential treatment was prohibited, requiring the court to construe it as discrimination lacking a proper basis under generally accepted actuarial standards.
scopes.why: The clause supplies no standard for what makes discrimination “unfair,” leaving the prohibited differential treatment indeterminate on its face.

scopes.issue: The phrase “class of insureds” was unclear as to whether classes had to be fixed when the policies were issued or could later be subdivided by age and face amount.
scopes.why: The phrase “any class of insureds” neither defines the classes nor states when they must be established or whether they may later be subdivided.

scopes.issue: The requirement to keep an “all risk policy” was disputed as to whether an empty-building policy could satisfy it, but the court held that the wording unambiguously required all-risk coverage of the specified property and improvements.
scopes.why: The clause itself requires an all-risk policy covering the specified personal property, buildings, and improvements, while identifying self-insurance only as a permitted method of furnishing that coverage.

scopes.issue: The indemnity for claims arising from accidents, injuries, or property damage at the Premises was unclear as to whether it covered Islip’s attorneys’ fees in direct litigation with Gander Mountain or only fees arising from third-party claims.
scopes.why: The clause includes attorneys’ fees within broad indemnity language tied to accidents, injuries, and property damage but does not expressly state whether direct interparty litigation is covered.

scopes.issue: The indemnity for a breach of the tenant’s representations or warranties was disputed as to whether Gander Mountain’s challenge to the Lease’s validity triggered fee shifting in litigation between the contracting parties.
scopes.why: The reader must consult the tenant’s representations elsewhere in the Lease, particularly Section 20.3, to see that the tenant represented that the Lease was valid and binding.

scopes.issue: The prohibition against any right to “accelerate” rent was disputed as to whether Islip could nevertheless recover all future rent immediately by characterizing it as damages for Gander Mountain’s anticipatory breach.
scopes.why: The clause itself preserves liability for future rent and other damages while expressly denying the landlord any right to accelerate rent, exposing the characterization dispute.

scopes.issue: The phrase selecting Wyoming’s “substantive laws” was disputed as to whether it also selected Wyoming law for the threshold procedural choice-of-law inquiry.
scopes.why: The clause itself selects only Wyoming’s “substantive laws” and does not expressly extend that selection to procedural choice-of-law rules.

scopes.issue: Brenner contended that the phrase “any dispute” was ambiguous, while the court held that she had identified no ambiguity in those words.
scopes.why: The asserted ambiguity lies directly in the clause’s undefined phrase “any dispute.”

scopes.issue: The broad words “any mediation or suit,” without an exception for wrongful-death or negligence actions, were disputed as to whether the Wyoming forum requirement reached noncontract tort claims.
scopes.why: The clause’s unqualified reference to “any mediation or suit” facially raises whether it encompasses noncontract tort actions.

scopes.issue: The phrase requiring suit “only in the State of Wyoming” was unclear about the court system, and the court construed it to permit either Wyoming state court or the federal District of Wyoming.
scopes.why: The words “in the State of Wyoming” specify geography but not whether suit must proceed in state or federal court.

scopes.issue: The phrases “field or prevailing area” and “whichever is the greater” left unclear whether royalties required the highest price from two distinct locations or merely imposed a field-based floor on Chesapeake’s actual downstream sales proceeds.
scopes.why: The wording “field or prevailing area whichever is the greater” itself leaves unclear whether “field” and “prevailing area” identify two comparison locations or a single synonymous geographic concept.

scopes.issue: The minimum-proceeds sentence’s relationship to the preceding actual-proceeds and expense provisions and the plant-residue cross-reference made unclear whether it redefined the royalty base or only protected against reductions caused by regulated-pipeline transportation costs.
scopes.why: The defect depends on comparing this sentence with paragraph 3(b)’s preceding actual-proceeds and expense provisions and paragraph 3(d)’s cross-reference applying it to plant-residue royalties.

scopes.issue: The definition combining claims arising directly or indirectly from the Agreement with representative and class claims required consideration within the Arbitration Provision as a whole to determine whether Pond’s tort and statutory class claims were covered.
scopes.why: The definition identifies covered categories, but the other provisions of the same Arbitration Provision are needed to determine whether those defined disputes must be arbitrated and how representative claims are treated.

scopes.issue: The broad definition of “Claim,” including disputes arising from the parties’ actions and requests for damages, penalties, or equitable relief, required consideration within the arbitration agreement as a whole to determine whether Vine’s claims were covered.
scopes.why: The definition establishes what qualifies as a “Claim,” but the same agreement’s operative arbitration and class-participation provisions are needed to determine whether and how Vine’s claims are covered.

scopes.issue: The definition’s authorization for MTC to revise the listed CAIs in its sole discretion made the allegedly promised total of 1,392 variable when the Network Operator Agreement was read as a whole, undermining Axia’s claim that the shortfall destroyed the agreements’ foundation.
scopes.why: Other provisions of the Network Operator Agreement supply the planned 1,392-CAI total whose status is affected by the definition’s revision power.

scopes.issue: The command to continue performing while a dispute is resolved was disputed as to whether it barred Axia from withholding performance based on MTC’s alleged material breach, and the court held that it did.
scopes.needs: 252FSupp3d52_guaranty_agreement
scopes.why: Without the Guaranty, the reader cannot see why Section 11.2 binds Axia NetMedia as guarantor or bars it from withholding guaranteed performance.

scopes.issue: The continued-performance provision’s relationship to dispute resolution had to be determined together with the Guaranty’s incorporation language, and the court held that the provision was incorporated into the Guaranty.
scopes.needs: 252FSupp3d52_guaranty_agreement
scopes.why: The Guaranty’s incorporation language is necessary to determine whether the Network Operator Agreement’s continued-performance provision became part of the Guaranty.

scopes.issue: The phrase “all other provisions relating to dispute resolution” was disputed as to whether it encompassed the Network Operator Agreement’s continued-performance provision, and the court held that it did.
scopes.needs: 252FSupp3d52_agreement_for_network_operator
scopes.why: The reader must see Section 11.2 of the Network Operator Agreement to determine whether it is an incorporated provision relating to dispute resolution.

scopes.issue: The opening mediation language was construed to make failed mediation or inability to convene it within 60 days a prerequisite to MTC’s election of arbitration, rendering the motion to compel premature.
scopes.needs: April 28,2017 mediation letter and motion-filing chronology
scopes.why: The clause establishes the mediation prerequisite, but the reader needs the parties’ mediation efforts and timing to see that the prerequisite was unsatisfied when MTC moved to compel.

scopes.issue: The incorporation sentence’s placement outside the Guaranty’s covenants article and under a heading omitting “dispute resolution” was argued to prevent it from imposing continued performance, but the court read the section and document as a whole and rejected that limitation.
scopes.why: The Guaranty’s article structure and section heading are needed to see that Section 4.6 sits outside the covenants article under a heading omitting “dispute resolution.”

scopes.issue: The phrase “subject to annual review for adjustment at the discretion of the Board” was disputed as to whether an annual salary review was mandatory while only an adjustment was discretionary, or whether the Board could decline to consider an adjustment altogether.
scopes.why: The wording itself leaves uncertain whether “at the discretion of the Board” modifies the obligation to conduct an annual review or only the decision to make an adjustment.

scopes.issue: The parenthetical “subject to approval by the Board and the Corporation’s policies” was ambiguous as to whether it conditioned Lankau’s individual stock-option eligibility or award on further approval, or referred only to Board approval of the stock-option plan itself.
scopes.why: The parenthetical’s placement and wording leave its approval condition uncertain between approval of the Stock Option Plan and further approval of the executive’s individual eligibility or award.

scopes.issue: The undefined phrase “oil and/or gas” made it disputed whether the royalty obligation covered liquid NGLs, which the court held were excluded under the ordinary meaning of “gas.”
scopes.why: The clause limits royalties to proceeds from “oil and/or gas” without stating whether that phrase includes liquid NGLs, so the coverage issue is visible from its wording alone.

scopes.issue: The phrase “Forgery or alteration of a Financial Instrument” was unclear as to whether “of a Financial Instrument” limited both forgery and alteration or only alteration, which would permit any forgery to trigger coverage.
scopes.why: The coordination in “Forgery or alteration of a Financial Instrument” itself permits uncertainty over whether “of a Financial Instrument” modifies both nouns or only “alteration.”

scopes.issue: The requirement of a “direct loss” resulting from computer fraud was disputed as to whether the intervening telephone call and employees’ approval steps broke the causal connection between the spoofed emails and the wire transfer.
scopes.needs: Evidence of the telephone call,spoofed emails,and employee approval steps
scopes.why: Without the transaction sequence, a reader could not assess whether those intervening acts broke the direct causal connection required by the clause.

scopes.issue: The requirement that the fraudulently induced transfer result from a Computer Violation was disputed as to whether the spoofed emails were sufficiently causal when Medidata employees themselves completed the transfer.
scopes.needs: Evidence of how the spoofed emails induced the employees to complete the transfer
scopes.why: The clause does not reveal the case-specific causal chain between the Computer Violation and Medidata’s employee-executed transfer.

scopes.issue: The phrase “fraudulent entry of Data into ... a Computer System” was disputed as to whether spoofed emails constituted deceitful unauthorized entry even though Medidata’s inbox was open to public email and no conventional hacking occurred.
scopes.needs: Evidence of the spoofing method,Medidata’s open inbox,and access to its email system
scopes.why: Whether the emails constituted deceitful unauthorized entry rather than ordinary receipt of public email depends on how the attack and system actually operated.

scopes.issue: The phrase “change to Data elements or program logic” was disputed as to whether embedded spoofing code that caused Gmail to display the president’s address and profile changed data or merely prompted the system to process the email normally.
scopes.needs: Technical evidence about the spoofing code and Gmail’s processing and display behavior
scopes.why: The clause alone cannot show whether the code changed data or merely caused Gmail to process and display the message normally.

scopes.issue: The definition’s reference to “signing” another person’s name was disputed as to whether a spoofed email displaying Medidata’s president’s name constituted an electronically produced forged signature.
scopes.needs: The spoofed emails and evidence of how the president’s name was displayed
scopes.why: Whether the displayed name was an electronically produced signature depends on the form and operation of the actual emails.

scopes.issue: The phrase “purportedly issued by an Organization” was disputed as to whether transfer instructions actually entered by Medidata employees could still be purportedly issued by Medidata when an impostor posing as its president directed those employees.
scopes.needs: Evidence that Medidata employees entered the transfer after receiving the impostor’s directions
scopes.why: The distinction between instructions actually and purportedly issued by Medidata turns on who created, communicated, and entered the transaction instructions.

scopes.issue: The phrase “without such Organization’s knowledge or consent” was disputed as to whether Medidata consented when its employees deliberately initiated and approved the transfer but did so only because their authorization was procured by trick.
scopes.needs: Evidence of the employees’ initiation and approval of the transfer and the deception procuring them
scopes.why: Whether Medidata consented despite its employees’ deliberate actions depends on the case-specific facts showing that their authorization was obtained by trick.

scopes.issue: The provision charging hourly rates only for services outside the defined scope had to be reconciled with the fees provision to determine whether in-scope services were compensated by hourly billing or a flat monthly fee.
scopes.why: Sections 1.1 and 4.1 are needed to identify the in-scope services and determine whether their compensation is hourly or a flat monthly retainer.

scopes.issue: The 60-day written-notice requirement had to be reconciled with the client’s right to stop work to determine whether compensation continued until formal termination.
scopes.why: The termination clause must be read with sections 4.1 and 6.1 to determine whether stopping work ends compensation before formal termination.

scopes.issue: The term “monthly retainer” was disputed as meaning either a flat monthly fee or an advance deposit against billable work.
scopes.why: The phrase “monthly retainer,” reinforced by the same clause’s hour-tracking requirement, itself presents the disputed flat-fee versus advance-deposit meanings.

scopes.issue: The flat-fee meaning of “monthly retainer” appeared in tension with the hour-tracking and invoice-detail requirements and therefore had to be resolved by reading the compensation scheme as a whole.
scopes.why: The clause itself juxtaposes a fixed “monthly retainer” with requirements to track all hours and provide invoice detail.

scopes.issue: The references to invoicing “for Services” and providing a detailed summary of “billable time” appeared to condition compensation on actual hourly work, but the court construed them with the retainer provision as accounting and payment-timing requirements rather than hourly billing terms.
scopes.why: The apparent hourly-work condition becomes an issue only when the invoice language is compared with section 4.1’s monthly-retainer compensation provision.

scopes.issue: The client’s right to stop work had to be reconciled with the flat monthly fee and written-termination provisions to decide whether stopping work also stopped the client’s payment obligation.
scopes.why: Whether stopping work ends payment requires reading this clause’s continuing-payment language with the flat-fee provision in section 4.1 and the formal-termination requirement in section 2.2.

scopes.issue: The phrase excluding investment depreciation caused by market fluctuation “unrelated to any Wrongful Act” was disputed as unclear in its application to losses allegedly caused by the officers’ wrongful investment decisions.
scopes.why: The clause itself makes the exclusion depend on whether market fluctuation is “unrelated to any Wrongful Act,” leaving unclear how it applies when both market movement and an alleged wrongful investment decision contribute to the loss.

scopes.issue: The words excluding claims brought “by, on behalf of, or at the behest of the Company” were disputed as unclear as to whether they encompass claims brought by the FDIC as the failed bank’s receiver.
scopes.why: The clause’s undefined relational phrases “by, on behalf of, or at the behest of the Company” themselves leave uncertain whether a receiver asserting the failed company’s claims falls within the exclusion.

scopes.issue: The phrase prohibiting Texhoma from directly or indirectly offering or providing services at covered sites was disputed as either a business-wide restraint applying by any means or a narrower restriction on using the Texhoma Fiber Route’s fibers.
scopes.why: The narrower fiber-use interpretation depends on the Lease Agreement’s provisions identifying the transaction, route, sites, and leased fibers; the quoted clause itself regulates services at covered sites without tying the prohibition to a particular means.

scopes.issue: The authorization for Texhoma to “assign its rights and obligations” was disputed as to whether it merely permitted delegation or also released Texhoma from its continuing contractual obligations, although it did not expressly provide for termination or release.
scopes.why: The clause authorizes assignment of “rights and obligations” but contains no language terminating or releasing Texhoma’s own obligations, making the delegation-versus-release issue visible from its wording alone.

scopes.issue: Reading the assignment provision with the written-agreement requirement and the non-circumvention covenant’s protective purpose defeated an implied-release interpretation that would let Texhoma retain fibers while escaping the restriction on their use.
scopes.why: The implied-release problem requires comparing § 18.10 with the same Lease Agreement’s written-agreement requirement, non-circumvention covenant, and provisions showing the covenant’s fiber-network purpose.

scopes.issue: The reference to a “delinquent Employer” owing expenses and interest for “such payment” was disputed as to whether it covered overdue withdrawal-liability payments or only delinquent employer contributions.
scopes.why: The competing readings depend on Article Nine’s surrounding provisions, which connect §§ 9.4–9.6 to employer contributions while addressing withdrawal liability separately in § 9.10.

scopes.issue: The phrase “8% of each employee’s pay rate per shift for each shift worked” was ambiguous as to whether the contribution base unit was each shift or the wages earned across those shifts.
scopes.why: The wording “8% of each employee’s pay rate per shift for each shift worked” itself permits the contribution base to be understood as either shifts or wages.

scopes.issue: The broad promise to arbitrate “any controversy or dispute” arising between “you and Wells Fargo Advisors,” while not expressly addressing class proceedings or containing a class waiver, was susceptible to competing individual-only and class-wide readings.
scopes.why: The clause itself broadly covers “any controversy or dispute,” uses bilateral “you and Wells Fargo Advisors” language, and says nothing expressly about class proceedings or a class waiver, exposing the competing readings.

scopes.issue: The broad promise to arbitrate “any controversy or dispute” arising between “you and Wells Fargo Advisors,” while not expressly addressing class proceedings or containing a class waiver, was susceptible to competing individual-only and class-wide readings.
scopes.why: The clause itself broadly covers “any controversy or dispute,” uses bilateral “you and Wells Fargo Advisors” language, and says nothing expressly about class proceedings or a class waiver, exposing the competing readings.

scopes.issue: The statement that Termination Value would reflect changes in the market value of the parties’ positions was unclear as to whether the defined Market Value of the MBS was an input Barclays could determine itself.
